name: Mai Tai
variant: 1944 original, Trader Vic's Oakland (17-year J. Wray & Nephew)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: juice of one fresh lime (one spent shell kept for garnish)

source: Victor Bergeron's own published account of the 1944 formula (as quoted in Trader Vic's later writings and by Jeff Berry)
notes: Vic built this in 1944 around a single aged Jamaican rum, using orgeat and orange curaçao as a nutty-orange sweetener pair and only a quarter ounce of rock candy syrup. Shaken with shaved ice and dumped unstrained, the spent lime shell and mint sprig are meant to look like an island with a palm tree. Don the Beachcomber later claimed the drink derived from his Q.B. Cooler, a claim Vic disputed.

name: Mai Tai
variant: Trader Vic's second formula, 1950s (1 oz Jamaican + 1 oz Martinique rum; Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: gold Jamaican rum (Vic used his own Trader Vic Jamaican)

source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007), after Trader Vic's post-17-year-rum formula (published in Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972)
notes: When the 17-year Wray & Nephew ran out (and a 15-year stopgap after it), Vic split the rum between a Jamaican and a Martinique rum to imitate its weight and funk. This two-rum Mai Tai is the template most modern bars follow.

name: Menehune Juice
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947-72 editions)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: 1 lime, squeezed over shaved ice; one shell saved
Trader Vic light Puerto Rican rum

source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947, revised 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A Mai Tai built on light Puerto Rican rum instead of aged Jamaican, so the orgeat and curaçao sit in front. Vic's menu line promised that one sip might let you see a Menehune, the little people of Hawaiian legend.

name: Honi Honi
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972 (Mai Tai template with bourbon)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972); proportions follow Vic's Mai Tai template (Difford's adaptation trims the lime)
notes: The name means 'kiss kiss'; it is Vic's Mai Tai skeleton with bourbon swapped in for rum. Vic ran several spirit-swap versions of the Mai Tai (bourbon, tequila, light rum), and this is the whiskey one.

name: Pinky Gonzales
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972 (tequila Mai Tai)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: rock candy syrup (Make and Drink's reading substitutes agave syrup)

source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972) via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription; cross-checked with Everyday Drinkers' version
notes: Vic's tequila Mai Tai, one of many tequila drinks in his 1972 revised guide, which gave agave spirits far more space than earlier bar books. The 2 : 1 : ½ : ¼ : ¼ proportions are the same as his other spirit-swap Mai Tais.

name: Space Needle
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972) via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: A big two-rum Mai Tai relative that swaps lime for lemon and doubles the curaçao; the name points to Seattle's 1962 World's Fair, where Trader Vic's had a presence. Date and venue are inferred from the name.

name: Scorpion
variant: 1946 punch-bowl recipe for about 12 (Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: 1 1/2 bottles Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito or Brugal); fifth-size bottles assumed
2 sprigs mint, steeped with the punch

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 77, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Vic's first printed Scorpion is a make-ahead punch: rum with a little gin and brandy, lots of lemon, orange and orgeat, stretched with white wine and left on cracked ice for two hours. He credited the idea to a Honolulu punch originally made with okolehao (ti-root spirit).

name: Scorpion
variant: Individual serving, Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972)
notes: The single-glass Scorpion drops the gin and wine of the 1946 punch and keeps a 2:1 rum-to-brandy base with orange, lemon and orgeat. It is spindle-mixed with a scoop of shaved ice, then poured over ice cubes.

name: Scorpion Bowl
variant: Bowl for a group, Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as summarized by Vintage American Cocktails
notes: The communal Scorpion as served in Trader Vic's restaurants, blended with two scoops of shaved ice and poured into a ceramic bowl with long straws. The book does not give a head count; servings=4 is an estimate by volume (about 2.5 individual Scorpions' worth of liquid before dilution).

name: Fog Cutter
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946) / Bartender's Guide (1947)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito, Boca Chica or Brugal)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), via the Food Timeline; same spec in the 1947 and 1972 Bartender's Guides
notes: Rum, brandy and gin stacked on a lemon-heavy orgeat base, with a sherry float that adds a nutty top note. Vic warned it was a 'triple threat', and the 1972 guide added his line that after two of these you won't even see the fog.

name: Samoan Fog Cutter
variant: 1950s lighter, blended version (Berry, Total Tiki)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: cream sherry (e.g. Harvey's Bristol Cream), floated

source: Jeff Berry, Total Tiki / Beachbum Berry Remixed, after Trader Vic c. 1950s
notes: Vic toned down his Fog Cutter by cutting the rum to 1½ oz and the brandy to ½ oz and flash-blending it with crushed ice. It became the version on Trader Vic's menus, served in its own tall ceramic mug.

name: Eastern Sour
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: juice of 1/2 orange (shell added to glass)
juice of 1/2 lemon (shell added to glass)

source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947); proportions per Jeff Berry and Make and Drink / Jason Miller readings of the book
notes: A whiskey sour done the Trader Vic way: orange juice lengthens it and a quarter ounce of orgeat plus sugar rounds it out, with the squeezed fruit shells left in the glass. Readings of 'half an orange' range from 1½ to 2½ oz, so the orange amount here is a midpoint.

name: London Sour
variant: 1963, Trader Vic's at the London Hilton (Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: Vic's Scotch counterpart to the Eastern Sour, made for the opening of his London restaurant in the Hilton on Park Lane in 1963. It is orange-dominant and only lightly sweetened with orgeat.

name: Potted Parrot
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947-72)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: orange curaçao (Difford's adaptation uses triple sec)

glass: Potted Parrot mug or sling glass
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947-72), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A long light-rum drink that is effectively a Menehune Juice lengthened with orange and lemon, the Mai Tai and Scorpion templates merged. It stayed on Trader Vic's menus for decades, served in a parrot-shaped mug.

name: Trader Vic Grog
variant: Trader Vic's (Berry, Grog Log / Total Tiki)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: dark Jamaican rum (Smuggler's Cove uses a blended overproof rum)

source: Trader Vic via Jeff Berry (Grog Log, Total Tiki); cross-checked with Martin Cate's spec in Easy Tiki and the TikiBot dataset
notes: Vic's house grog is not a Navy Grog copy: dark rum with equal parts lemon, pineapple and passion fruit syrup, sharpened with a heavy dose of Angostura. It is a simple 2 : 1 : 1 : 1 structure.

name: Navy Grog
variant: Trader Vic's version (Bartender's Guide rev. / Rum Cookery & Drinkery, 1970s)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: third, lighter blended rum (modern readings use Chairman's Reserve or a light blended rum)

source: Trader Vic's 1970s Navy Grog as reproduced by Anders Erickson and discussed by Vintage American Cocktails / The Lost Tiki Lounge; structure cross-checked with Smuggler's Cove
notes: Where Don the Beachcomber sweetened his Navy Grog with honey and added soda, Vic's version splits the sweetener between demerara syrup and pimento dram, which gives it an allspice edge. At the restaurants it was built from his bottled Navy Grog mix, and it became the best-known grog of the 1960s and 70s.

name: Tiki Puka Puka
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972); Navy Grog mix reconstructed
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: part of 3 oz Trader Vic Navy Grog Mix (reconstructed)
part of 3 oz Trader Vic Navy Grog Mix (reconstructed)
part of 3 oz Trader Vic Navy Grog Mix (reconstructed)
part of 3 oz Trader Vic Navy Grog Mix (reconstructed)

source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as reported by Cocktail Virgin Slut; the Navy Grog mix is split using the lime : grapefruit : demerara : pimento ratio of Vic's Navy Grog
notes: Vic's three-rum strong drink (light, dark Jamaican and 151 Demerara) is lengthened with orange juice and his bottled Navy Grog mix, then reddened with grenadine. The published recipe calls for 3 oz of the mix, and its breakdown into lime, grapefruit, demerara syrup and pimento dram here is a reconstruction. Trader Vic's current recipe is different, using orange, lemon, grenadine and only 1 oz of grog mix.

name: Doctor Funk
variant: Trader Vic's version, Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: dark Jamaica or Martinique rum (Red Heart, Myers's or Rum Negrita)
1 lime, halved and squeezed; shells dropped into the shaker

garnish: fruit or a fresh geranium leaf
source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 54, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Named for Dr. Bernard Funk, the German physician in Samoa whose absinthe, grenadine and lime tonic appears in South Seas travel writing. Vic's version is a strong dark-rum punch with a quarter ounce of Pernod, both lemon and lime, and a soda top.

name: Trader Vic Punch
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: dark Jamaica rum (Red Heart or Myers's)
Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito or Brugal)
1 slice pineapple, hand-shaken with the drink

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 69, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Vic's own house rum punch pairs dark Jamaican and light Puerto Rican rum over half an orange and half a lemon, with a pineapple slice and a touch of orgeat. It is shaken by hand with shaved ice and served unstrained, and the orgeat is an early sign of the Mai Tai's flavor pairing.

name: Planter's Punch
variant: Trader Vic's own version, Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 61, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Vic's personal Planter's Punch is a strong one, with 3 oz of dark Jamaican rum, lime plus lemon, and grenadine as nearly the only sweetener. It is stirred with large ice, poured over cracked ice and topped with soda.

name: Zombie
variant: Trader Vic's simplified home version, Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito or Brugal)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), pp. 70-71, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Vic openly credited the Zombie to Don the Beachcomber and printed this simpler version of his own: three rums with a full ounce of orange curaçao, lemon, orange and grenadine instead of Don's secret mixes. It is stirred rather than blended and poured over cracked ice.

name: Shingle Stain
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: dark Jamaican rum (Red Heart or Myers's)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), pp. 67-68, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: A short, rum-forward sour pairing dark Jamaican and Martinique rum, the same combination Vic later used for the Mai Tai, with a quarter ounce of pimento dram for spice. Almost all the sugar comes from the allspice liqueur and a dash of grenadine.

name: Mahukona
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946)

ingredients.orig: 2 dashes Angostura, put in the glass first and left unstirred
Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito or Brugal)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 56, as quoted by the Food Timeline; later in the 1972 guide
notes: A light, lower-proof pineapple-lemon rum sour that Vic said he had served for years, from a recipe scribbled on a scrap of paper whose origin he had forgotten. The bitters go into the glass first and are left unmixed, so they come through as a streak.

name: Wahine
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito, Boca Chica or Brugal)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 108, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Equal parts rum and pineapple juice over one large piece of ice in a coconut shell, which Vic suggested for hostesses entertaining at luncheon. It is about the simplest possible tropical drink and an early coconut-shell presentation.

name: Tortuga
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946) / Bartender's Guide (1947)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: 2 dashes crème de cacao (modern readings: 3/8-1/2 oz)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946) / Bartender's Guide (1947, unchanged in 1972), via Cocktail Virgin Slut and Vintage American Cocktails
notes: Two overproof rums (Cuban and 151 Demerara) with sweet vermouth, three citrus juices, and chocolate-orange accents from cacao and curaçao. Jeff Berry thinks Vic modeled it on the Havana La Florida cocktail. The book lists the liqueurs as 'dashes', which modern makers read as roughly 3/8 to 1/2 oz each.

name: Myrtle Bank Punch
variant: As recorded in Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947); Berry reading
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947) as reprinted by Jeff Berry (from memory of Beachbum Berry Remixed; not re-verified online); Difford's gives a different Jamaican-rum/Heering spec
notes: A Jamaican hotel punch that Vic recorded: a short shot of overproof rum sharpened with lime and grenadine, with a cherry-liqueur float. Vic's books also printed the hotel's Northside Special, which shows how much the Kingston hotel bars shaped his early drinks.

name: El Diablo
variant: 'Mexican El Diablo', Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: juice of 1/2 lime; squeezed shell dropped in the glass

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), in Smuggler's Cove's reading
notes: One of the earliest tequila highballs in an American bar book: tequila, lime and crème de cassis topped with ginger ale over cracked ice. It later became a modern-classic standard, usually made with ginger beer.

name: Honolulu
variant: Trader Vic's (Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972, 'one of the first drinks we ever originated')
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: fresh pineapple (about half a slice), blended

source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972) via Make and Drink transcription and Difford's adaptation
notes: A blended pink pineapple daiquiri that Vic marked with his TV logo and said was among the very first drinks the Oakland bar originated. It is unrelated to the older gin-based Honolulu Cocktail.

name: Tonga Punch
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: A light-rum orange punch sharpened with both lemon and lime and lightly sweetened with curaçao and grenadine. It is typical of the easygoing citrus punches that filled out Vic's menus.

name: Rum Keg
variant: Trader Vic's, served in a ceramic keg for sharing
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: A communal punch of mostly light rum with lemon, pineapple, passion fruit and apricot liqueur, served in Trader Vic's small ceramic kegs. The four-serving count comes from the transcription.

name: Kava Bowl
variant: Trader Vic c. 1942 (Berry, Intoxica!), single-serve adaptation
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Difford's Guide adaptation of the Trader Vic recipe in Jeff Berry's Intoxica! (2002)
notes: A pineapple-lemon light-rum punch named after the Polynesian kava ceremony, which also inspired Vic's communal Scorpion bowls. Only Difford's single-serve adaptation was available, so the original bowl proportions are unconfirmed.

name: Hinky Dinks Fizzy
variant: 1984, Trader Vic's 50th anniversary (Smuggler's Cove spec)
creator: Trader Vic's (company)
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016)
notes: Made for Trader Vic's 50th anniversary and named after Hinky Dink's, the Oakland saloon Vic opened in 1934. Gin and rum go over pineapple, passion fruit and apricot, and the drink is poured onto sparkling wine in a snifter.

name: Aku Aku
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), Smuggler's Cove adaptation
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: blended lightly aged rum (orig. light rum)

garnish: large mint leaf or small mint sprig cluster
source: Smuggler's Cove (2016), adapting Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972); cross-checked with Difford's
notes: A blended, double-strained pineapple-mint daiquiri with a little peach, close kin to Don the Beachcomber's Missionary's Downfall. It is served up, which is unusual for a tiki drink.

name: Kama'aina
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: A gin-and-coconut cooler lifted with 7-Up. The name is Hawaiian for a long-time island resident. It shows Vic's later habit of combining cream of coconut with citrus and soda.

name: Bourbon Special
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription; also listed in Berry's Total Tiki
notes: A short bourbon sour spiced with falernum and Angostura and topped with a splash of ginger beer. It shows how Vic applied tiki modifiers to whiskey for customers who didn't drink rum.

name: Western Sour
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription; also listed in Berry's Total Tiki
notes: The counterpart to Vic's Eastern Sour: bourbon lengthened with grapefruit instead of orange and sweetened with falernum instead of orgeat.

name: Montego Bay
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972, TV-logo original)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A Martinique-rum daiquiri with triple sec and bitters, marked in Vic's guide as a house original. The Jamaican name despite the French-island rum is typical of Vic's loose use of Caribbean place names.

name: Tahitian Honey Bee
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A light-rum honey sour, essentially a rum Bee's Knees made with lemon. Honey was a common Polynesian-bar sweetener, and here it is the only one.

name: Shark's Tooth
variant: Trader Vic's No. 1 (Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972: 'one of the first drinks we ever made')
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: Vic's own Shark's Tooth, distinct from Don the Beachcomber's, is a strong rum rickey with both lemon and lime, a touch of grenadine and soda. Vic said it was among the first drinks made at Hinky Dink's.

name: Pino Pepe
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), served in a pineapple shell
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A frozen rum-and-vodka pineapple drink served in a hollowed pineapple, one of the showpiece presentations of Trader Vic's 1960s and 70s menus. Vodka appears as Vic's menus caught up with American tastes of the time.

name: Tabu
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972; 'originated in Seattle')
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A frozen pineapple-lemon drink split between light rum and vodka, which Vic said came from his Seattle restaurant. It is plain and fruity, typical of the vodka-friendly 1960s menus.

name: Banana Cow
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947); Make and Drink transcription and Difford's adaptation
notes: A blended banana-milk rum shake with a dash each of vanilla and Angostura, and Vic's cold variation on the old milk punch. Difford's credits it as a Bergeron creation.

name: Hot Rum Cow
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: Hot milk, light rum, sugar and a dash each of vanilla and Angostura, frothed in the spindle mixer and topped with nutmeg. It is the hot form of Vic's Rum Cow.

name: Hot Brown Cow
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: Equal parts hot milk and strong coffee spiked with Jamaican rum and dusted with nutmeg: a café-au-lait version of the Rum Cow, and unsweetened.
